title: Imbalanced Data Problem in Machine Learning: A Review
authors: Altalhan, M.; Algarni, A.; Alouane, M.
tldr: A comprehensive survey reviews 40 studies on machine learning techniques for handling imbalanced data, covering data-level, algorithm-level, and hybrid strategies alongside evaluation metrics for imbalanced classification.
problem_and_motivation: Class imbalance in datasets causes classifiers to become biased toward the majority class, leading to poor minority class recognition in critical domains such as healthcare diagnosis and fraud detection. Existing data-level and algorithm-level techniques each have inherent limitations that reduce their standalone effectiveness. A systematic understanding of these approaches, their limitations, and appropriate evaluation metrics is needed to guide robust model development.
approach: Surveyed 40 studies from Google Scholar, IEEE, Springer, Elsevier, and MDPI, focusing on publications from 2020 to 2024.
Organized techniques into three categories: data-level, algorithm-level, and hybrid approaches.
Reviewed oversampling methods including SMOTE, ADASYN, Borderline-SMOTE, and their variants.
Reviewed undersampling methods including Random Undersampling, Tomek Links, and Cluster Centroids.
Covered algorithm-level strategies including cost-sensitive learning, algorithm-specific adjustments, and ensemble methods.
Examined hybrid approaches combining data-level and algorithm-level techniques across real-world domains.
Analyzed evaluation metrics including AUC, F1 Score, G-mean, and AUPRC for imbalanced classification.
Identified persistent gaps in generalizability, scalability, and robustness across all technique categories.
findings: Data-level techniques risk overfitting from synthetic samples or information loss from undersampling.
Algorithm-level techniques may not fully exploit available data or require complex per-algorithm adjustments.
Hybrid approaches combining multiple strategies best mitigate overfitting, information loss, and poor minority class performance.
Accuracy is unreliable for imbalanced datasets as a model can achieve high accuracy by classifying all instances as majority class.
AUPRC outperforms AUC for highly imbalanced big data because AUC fails to capture precision scores and false positive counts.
num: 40 studies reviewed across data-level, algorithm-level, and hybrid technique categories.
GAN-based methods are gaining traction but are susceptible to mode collapse and demand substantial computational resources.
Cost-sensitive learning methods like ACL dynamically adapt sample costs throughout the training process.
num: Most reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2024 from Q1 and Q2 ranked journals.
Persistent gaps remain in scalability, generalizability, and robustness across data-level, algorithmic, and hybrid approaches.
key_figures_tables: Table 1: Effectiveness and limitations of hybrid-sampling techniques → Summarizes trade-offs of SMOTE variants and hybrid sampling methods.
Table 2: Effectiveness and limitations of ensemble methods → Compares boosting, bagging, and deep ensemble approaches for imbalance.
Table 3: Effectiveness and limitations of hybrid approaches → Shows combined data-level and algorithm-level technique trade-offs.
Table 4: Applications of hybrid approaches → Maps real-world domains (healthcare, fraud, cybersecurity) to specific hybrid methods.
Table 5: Evaluation metrics for imbalance classification → Lists metrics derived from confusion matrix for imbalanced evaluation.

definitions.definition: Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique that generates new minority samples by interpolating between nearest neighbors.
Adaptive Synthetic Sampling, a variant of SMOTE that adaptively generates more synthetic samples for harder-to-learn minority instances.
Area Under the ROC Curve, a metric summarizing classifier performance across all threshold settings.
Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve, a more effective metric than AUC for highly imbalanced big data.
Geometric Mean of Recall and Specificity, ensuring balanced performance across both classes.
Generative Adversarial Network, a model with a generator and discriminator that creates synthetic data samples.
Gradient Boosting Decision Trees, an ensemble method that iteratively builds trees to correct prior errors.
True Positives: correctly identified positive observations.
True Negatives: correctly identified negative observations.
False Positives: incorrectly identified as positive.
False Negatives: incorrectly identified as negative.
Adaptive Cost-Sensitive Learning, a method that dynamically adapts sample costs during training to handle imbalanced data.
Maximum Mean Discrepancy, a statistical measure used in transfer learning to align source and target domain distributions.
Receiver Operating Characteristic curve, graphing True Positive Rate against False Positive Rate across threshold configurations.
Multiple Kernel Learning, a technique allowing SVMs to integrate and weight different kernel functions for classification.
Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network, used for generating synthetic samples in imbalanced datasets.
Modified Convolutional Neural Network, used in the Active Balancing Mechanism for medical data classification.
Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access, a telecommunications technique where class imbalance handling improves user classification.
Particle Swarm Optimization, an attribute selection technique used in combination with resampling for imbalanced data.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This survey provides a systematic and comprehensive review of 40 studies on the imbalanced data problem in machine learning, organized across data-level, algorithm-level, and hybrid technique categories. It identifies specific strengths and limitations of each approach, including SMOTE variants, ensemble methods, cost-sensitive learning, and GAN-based data augmentation. The paper establishes that hybrid approaches combining multiple strategies most effectively mitigate overfitting, information loss, and poor minority class performance. It critically examines evaluation metrics, demonstrating that accuracy is unreliable for imbalanced datasets while AUPRC outperforms AUC for highly imbalanced big data. The survey identifies persistent research gaps in scalability, generalizability, and robustness across all technique categories.
directly_justifies: Hybrid approaches combining data-level and algorithm-level strategies most effectively mitigate overfitting, information loss, and poor minority class performance.
Accuracy is unreliable for imbalanced datasets because models achieve high accuracy by classifying all instances as majority class.
AUPRC outperforms AUC for highly imbalanced big data because AUC fails to capture precision scores and false positive counts.
SMOTE-generated synthetic samples may resemble majority instances, causing classifier confusion in high-overlap datasets.
Persistent gaps in scalability, generalizability, and robustness exist across data-level, algorithmic, and hybrid approaches.
limits: The survey does not address deep learning architectures specifically designed for temporal spending data.
No empirical benchmarking is performed; the review is purely based on surveyed literature findings.
The paper does not cover domain-specific techniques tailored for personal finance or budgeting systems.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned for relevance. Domain 8 (Anomaly Detection) was flagged as highly relevant because class imbalance is the central challenge in anomaly and fraud detection, making this survey directly applicable to understanding detection algorithms and baseline strategies. Domain 14 (Synthetic Data/ML Deployment) was flagged as relevant, with 14.A rated high due to comprehensive GAN and SMOTE coverage, while 14.B and 14.C received low and contextual ratings respectively due to only tangential discussion of computational costs. Domain 12 (Evaluation Frameworks) was flagged as relevant because the survey thoroughly analyzes metrics like AUC, F1, G-mean, and AUPRC for imbalanced classification evaluation. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) received medium relevance as the review discusses ensemble and deep learning predictive models. Domains 1-5 (demographics, financial structure, spending patterns, expense categorization, existing PF systems) were considered and rejected as the paper is a general ML survey with no personal finance domain specificity. Domain 7 (Budgeting), Domain 9 (Mobile-First), Domain 10 (Privacy/Security), Domain 11 (Engagement), and Domain 13 (Savings/Debt) were similarly rejected as irrelevant. Domain 3 (Expense Categorization) was considered due to the classification nature of imbalance work but rejected as the paper does not address expense categorization frameworks. The paper's overall topical coverage centers on anomaly detection algorithms, synthetic data generation for ML, and evaluation methodologies for imbalanced classification systems.

limitations: The survey is purely a literature review with no empirical benchmarking or experimental comparison of techniques.
Generalizability is limited as most reviewed techniques are evaluated on specific domains rather than across diverse domains.
The paper does not address deep learning architectures specifically designed for sequential or temporal imbalanced data.
Computational complexity analysis is discussed qualitatively but not systematically benchmarked across methods.
remember_this: Hybrid approaches combining data-level and algorithm-level techniques best mitigate overfitting, information loss, and minority class bias.
Accuracy is unreliable for imbalanced datasets where models can achieve 99 percent accuracy by classifying all instances as majority class.
AUPRC outperforms AUC for highly imbalanced big data because AUC fails to capture precision scores and false positive counts.
SMOTE variants may create ambiguous samples near decision boundaries when significant class overlap exists.
Persistent research gaps remain in scalability, generalizability, and robustness across all imbalance handling approaches.
